source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: First psychometric test of a c-like factor in LLM agent groups. 108 groups, 8 LLMs, 5 tasks. One general factor (ACI) appears.
numbers: 108 groups (sizes 3,5,8; rounds 2,3; decentralized, centralized, random topologies; homogeneous or mixed LLMs). Tasks: commonsense, math, game, coding, writing. First factor 66.3% of variance, second 18.7%. CFA one-factor chi2=30.6, CFI=0.967.
limits: Only 5 tasks, one debate-style framework, 2024-era models (gpt-3.5, gpt-4o-mini, Qwen2.5, GLM-4-9b, InternLM2.5, gemma-2-27b). Groups share one scaffold, so shared method variance may inflate the factor. No second lab replication yet.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring a scaffold's general quality across tasks, not one task. Background only for our single-agent schema.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Cross-task correlation of group scores is much higher for LLM groups than for human groups.
numbers: Mean cross-task r=0.55 for LLM groups versus r=0.28 in human groups (Riedl 2021); factor share 66.3% versus 43% in humans.
limits: Human figure is quoted from the paper (Riedl 2021 itself reports 0.27). Higher LLM correlation is probably because the same base models drive every task, so groups differ in model strength more than humans differ in ability.
agent_relevance: A general factor among LLM configurations may mostly be base-model strength. Test it by holding the model fixed.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: The factor predicts a held-out task. Leave-one-out ACI from four tasks predicts the fifth.
numbers: Correlations above 0.8 on three held-out tasks, about 0.5 on the other two, all p<0.001. Predicted ACI beats a simple average-of-four-tasks baseline.
limits: Held-out tasks are still in the same five-task family. Which two tasks were near 0.5 is only in a figure.
agent_relevance: A scaffold score from a few tasks can forecast others, so cheap proxy tasks may rank scaffold variants.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Collaboration process matters more than individual ability for ACI, echoing Riedl 2021. Skill congruence (strong agents on high-degree nodes) is the main driver.
numbers: Random forest importance: skill congruence over 50%, mean individual g 37%, max g, group size and effort each under 5%. Linear model: skill congruence and mean g significant positive; size and effort not. Variance of degree (like unequal speaking turns) was an indicator.
limits: Importance is from 108 groups; indicators correlated by design. Congruence defined as correlation of agent g with node degree.
agent_relevance: Put the stronger reasoner where most messages flow. More agents or more chatter does not help by itself.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: A stronger LLM does not guarantee a stronger group. Topology can beat model strength and cost.
numbers: Group 2 (Qwen2.5-72B, g=119.9) cost 75% more than group 1 (internlm2.5-20b, g=92.1) yet its ACI was 9.7% lower. Centralized network with the strongest LLM as hub beat the fully connected decentralized network in most cases at lower token cost.
limits: Case study of two groups, not a controlled sweep.
agent_relevance: Supports routing and hub design over bigger models; matches our scaffold-over-model premise.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Indicators of the group (no task runs needed) predict ACI and performance of unseen groups.
numbers: 2-fold cross-validated random forest: R2 over 0.8 for ACI, over 0.6 for most tasks. Best group is in the top 3 predictions for ACI, commonsense and game; math gives 100% best-group identification.
limits: Half-split CV on 108 groups from one generator; no outside configurations.
agent_relevance: Cheap structure-based prediction of agent-system quality before running it.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Using predicted ACI as a regulariser improved two topology optimisers on unseen tasks.
numbers: GPTSwarm: commonsense 0.75 to 0.77, math 0.81 to 0.91 (+12.3%), game 0.50 to 0.53, coding 0.87 to 0.89, writing 0.88 to 0.89. G-Designer gains 2.3% to 7.8%. Paper reports average +4.6%.
limits: Leave-one-out over only five tasks; ACI predictor trained on the same 108 groups; no variance or seeds shown. Table in the PDF has garbled rows for G-Designer.
agent_relevance: A general-ability prior can reduce overfitting of a scaffold to one benchmark. Relevant to our guard against benchmark overfit.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models (ICLR 2026)
finding: Multi-agent LLM groups playing a coordination-free guessing game show synergy and complementarity only with prompt steering. Parallel to c: alignment plus complementary roles.
numbers: GPT-4.1 groups of 3-15 at temperature 0-1: each extra member cuts success odds about 8% (OR=0.92); each unit of temperature raises odds about 50% (OR=1.50, p<1e-7). Three arms: Plain, Persona, Persona+ToM ('think about what other agents might do'). Only about 3.5% of Plain experiments individually significant for emergence; ToM arm shows more groups with significant higher-order information.
limits: One task (number-sum guessing game, Goldstone et al.), groups of N=10, order-2 synergy only. ToM mediation is marginal: ACME=0.034, 95% CI -0.000 to 0.07, p=0.053.
agent_relevance: A one-line theory-of-mind instruction changed group structure. Cheap to test in a multi-agent branch of our schema.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models (ICLR 2026)
finding: Synergy and redundancy together predict performance; neither alone does.
numbers: Interaction coefficient 0.24, p=0.014: redundancy raises the benefit of synergy by about 27% on the log-odds scale and vice versa.
limits: Observational regression with inverse probability weights; single task.
agent_relevance: Aligned goals plus complementary contributions is the working recipe; note this mirrors human c findings.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models (ICLR 2026)
finding: Replication across models: capable models show the effect; the small model fails.
numbers: GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1-70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3-235B reach similar success rates and show Persona/ToM emergence. Llama-3.1-8B largely fails to break oscillation. Qwen3 reasoning agents sometimes fall into endless chain of thought on noisy feedback.
limits: Model ToM capacity offered as explanation but not directly measured here.
agent_relevance: Group gains depend on a minimum per-agent capability, so test on the actual base model.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: Hidden-profile benchmark: multi-agent LLMs fail to pool distributed information, the opposite of the c-factor hope that groups integrate more than one member.
numbers: 65 tasks, 15 frontier LLMs, 10 sessions per task. Multi-agent accuracy 30.1% under distributed information versus 80.7% for single agents with full information. GPT-4.1 on the three verification tasks: 0.008 before talking, 0.233 after; full-profile 0.733.
limits: Tasks synthetic (GPT-4.1 generated; 57 of 200 candidates passed filter, 28.5%). Average-rule scoring of votes before and after discussion.
agent_relevance: Premature convergence on shared facts is the core failure. A scaffold should make agents ask what others know.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: Human comparison on the same tasks shows the same hidden-profile pattern, so the LLM failure is not a pure artifact.
numbers: Humans: pre-discussion 0.125 (hidden) versus 0.604 (full profile); post-discussion 0.385, below ceiling, p=0.003.
limits: Small human sample on three tasks; details in the paper appendix.
agent_relevance: LLM groups behave like humans in the classic Stasser-Titus failure but worse.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: Which prompts and structures changed results, and by how much (GPT-4.1).
numbers: Rounds 5/10/15/20: post accuracy 0.108/0.200/0.233/0.133. Prompts: cooperative 0.200-0.242, conflictual 0.017, zero-shot CoT 0.222, 'Informing Asymmetry' 0.367 (best, still far below full profile). One adversarial agent plus 3 default helped; more adversaries hurt (Goldilocks). Forced disclosure of all facts: 96.7%. Passive summarisation: 10%.
limits: Single model (GPT-4.1) for ablations. Group-size gains reverse as N grows.
agent_relevance: Targeted fix: surface unshared information, add one dissenter, do not just add rounds.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs (HiddenBench)
finding: Model scale and individual reasoning do not predict collective performance.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro best post-discussion hidden-profile accuracy 0.671 (gap to full 0.310); Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.550; Flash-Lite 0.394. GPT-5 variants no better than GPT-4.1-Mini in multi-agent settings.
limits: Family differences might reflect prompt or format sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Echoes the c-factor claim that group ability is not average member ability.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
finding: Teamwork benchmark for AI agents inspired by decades of human team measurement, scored only on tasks the model solves alone to separate teamwork from capability.
numbers: 240 tasks (160 public, 80 held out), 8 teamwork dimensions, 18 models. Best score 82.2/100. Models reach best deal in only 14% of conflicts. Pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when taking over after a weaker model cheated.
limits: Model names in the document are as printed (post-2025 names). Not a group-level c; each score is one model acting as teammate.
agent_relevance: Teammate quality is a separable trait. If our agent runs sub-agents, test them as teammates.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
finding: Capability explains most but not all teamwork. Same-capability models differ by up to 11 points.
numbers: Score versus Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index r=0.92 (95% CI 0.87-0.97), capability explains 85% of variance; HLE r=0.92; LMArena r=0.76. Two models 1 index point apart differ by 11 points as teammates.
limits: 17 models at one reasoning setting; correlation across models, not groups.
agent_relevance: Support for 'collaboration is not capability', the same message as human c.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
finding: A single component across the eight teamwork scores looks like a general factor, with one dimension (handling conflict) going the other way.
numbers: One component explains 71% of variance in the eight scores. Other dimensions correlate with each other r>=0.59; conflict correlates -0.43 to -0.23 with each, and r=-0.34 with capability.
limits: Principal component on 17-18 models; not a formal factor analysis with fit indices.
agent_relevance: Stronger models cave under interpersonal pressure. A scaffold needs an explicit hold-your-position step against sycophancy.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
finding: Social sensitivity is operationalised as an LLM task (a teammate who holds a key fact withdraws).
numbers: Task family 'emotional intelligence' tied explicitly to Woolley 2010 social sensitivity finding; other families: information sharing (hidden profile), resisting unsafe pressure, reporting misconduct, keeping on track, initiative.
limits: Pointer to Woolley 2010 is by citation; no c-factor extraction.
agent_relevance: Direct translation of the c-factor correlates into agent tests.

source: Huang et al. (2025) On the Dynamics of Multi-Agent LLM Communities Driven by Value Diversity
finding: Pilot study that treats c-factor ideas (balanced participation, diversity) as indicators in LLM communities.
numbers: Groups of 4, 10, 30 agents with Schwartz-values personas. Diminishing returns: 4 to 10 agents large gain, 10 to 30 smaller; extreme heterogeneity brings instability. Multi-value groups proposed 20-30% more high-quality rules; fully balanced value mix had the highest emergence scores, above no-value controls.
limits: Open-ended simulation, no task accuracy, emergence scores are authors' own metrics; no Woolley-style battery. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Persona diversity may help only up to a limit. Weak support for persona mixes in a multi-agent branch.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Large controlled scaling study shows there is no single general collaboration gain; effect depends on task structure.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures (single, independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid), 3 LLM families. Relative change from single-agent baseline from +80.8% (decomposable financial reasoning) to -70.0% (sequential planning). Predictive model cross-validated R2=0.373 (0.413 with capability metric); picks best architecture for 87% of held-out configs.
limits: Cuts against a strong unitary c: gains are task-structured. Benchmark set of six.
agent_relevance: Do not assume multi-agent helps by default; gate it by task decomposability.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Capability ceiling and error amplification.
numbers: Single-agent baseline above 45% gives negative returns from more agents (beta=-0.236, p=0.004). Error amplification: single 1.0, centralized 4.4, hybrid 5.1, decentralized 7.8, independent 17.2. Tool-heavy tasks incur overhead (beta=-0.096, p=0.002).
limits: Correlational regression across configurations.
agent_relevance: A central verifier contains errors; unchecked parallel agents amplify them.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: Failure taxonomy for multi-agent LLM systems; inter-agent misalignment is a main category, the failure c-factor research would call poor process.
numbers: 1642 annotated traces from 7 frameworks; failure rates 41% to 86.7%; 14 failure modes in 3 categories (design, inter-agent misalignment, verification). Annotator kappa=0.88. Disobey task spec about 11.8-15.2% of traces; information withholding is a listed mode.
limits: Open-source frameworks of 2024-25; counts depend on LLM-as-judge pipeline.
agent_relevance: Concrete process failure list to check for in any multi-agent branch.

source: Ruan et al. (2025) Benchmarking LLMs' Swarm Intelligence (SwarmBench)
finding: Swarm coordination benchmark: LLMs show weak decentralised coordination, with no model best on all tasks.
numbers: 5 tasks (Pursuit, Synchronization, Foraging, Flocking, Transport), 5x5 local view, mean of five runs. Flocking scored highest, Synchronization showed most divergence; gemini-2.0-flash and o4-mini good at spatial tasks, claude-3.7-sonnet at Synchronization.
limits: Cites Woolley 2010 only as motivation; no factor analysis, exact scores in a table not extracted. Physical group dynamics predicted success more than message semantics.
agent_relevance: Task-specific rather than general group skill; weakens a strong c for LLM swarms.

source: Riedl and Weidmann (2025) Quantifying Human-AI Synergy (project page, PsyArXiv preprint)
finding: Human-AI synergy measured by item response theory, separating solo ability and collaboration ability, plus theory of mind.
numbers: 667 participants; GPT-4o raises performance 29 percentage points, Llama-3.1-8B 23 points; low-ability users gain most. Solo ability and collaboration-with-AI ability are distinct latent traits; theory of mind predicts success with AI but not alone.
limits: Read from project page, not the full preprint; no coefficients reported on the page.
agent_relevance: Collaboration with AI is its own trait, parallel to c separate from g. Informs how an agent should model its partner.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups, PNAS
finding: Human anchor: the largest test of the c factor, with the process-over-skill result later copied in LLM papers.
numbers: 22 studies, 1,356 groups, 5,279 individuals, 4-8 tasks per study. Mean inter-task r=0.27 (0.12-0.50). Loadings 0.27-0.52; average variance extracted 44%. Leave-one-out prediction of a held-out task average r=0.40 (0.26-0.53). Collaboration process (skill congruence, strategy, effort) explains most CI, then individual skill, then composition; proportion of women acts through social perceptiveness.
limits: Corrected in PNAS 2022. Tasks administered on one platform (POGS), computer mediated; correlations modest.
agent_relevance: The skill-congruence and process findings are what the ACI paper tests in LLMs.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) AI-Augmented Co-Design in Healthcare: Log-Based Markers of Teamwork and Collective Intelligence, Behav Sci
finding: A small AI process-assistant study uses turn-taking balance as a CI marker for human teams.
numbers: Six four-person teams; assistant nudged timing, turn-taking and hand-offs. Expert rating mean 4.18/5, perceived performance 6.14/7. Balanced participation and clearer pacing tended to go with better performance; more turns did not.
limits: Descriptive only, n=6 teams, no c-factor extraction.
agent_relevance: Equal participation as a monitorable signal; shows an AI actor steering turn-taking.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups, Science
finding: Founding study (recalled from prior knowledge, not opened this session). 192 groups of 2-5, 699 people, 12 tasks in two studies; first factor explained about 43% of variance.
numbers: Study 1: 40 groups, 2-3 members; study 2: 152 groups, 3-5 members. c correlated with average social sensitivity (about r=0.26), equality of turn-taking (about r=0.41), proportion of women (about r=0.23); average and maximum member intelligence correlated only about 0.15 and 0.19. Predicted criterion tasks better than member IQ.
limits: Numbers from memory; verify before citing. Later critiques are in the sibling subfield 08.
agent_relevance: Source of the turn-taking and social sensitivity ideas used in LLM group tests.

source: Burton et al. (2024) How large language models can reshape collective intelligence, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Review of how LLMs can help or harm collective intelligence (abstract-level knowledge only; Woolley is coauthor). Cited by the value-diversity paper as part of the LLM collective intelligence line.
numbers: No new measurements; framework paper with risks such as homogenisation of views and opportunities in deliberation and aggregation.
limits: Paywalled; not opened.
agent_relevance: Reminder that LLM use can reduce diversity, which c-style groups need.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups, PNAS
finding: Gap: no direct replication of the ACI factor in LLM groups by another lab was found, nor any LLM study using Woolley's original 12-task battery with turn-taking and social sensitivity measured. Search budget was limited; arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited.
numbers: none
limits: Gap statement, not a finding.
agent_relevance: Open question for our work: an independent replication of the 66.3% factor with a fixed base model.
